In reality and normal use, every node can join and follow one of three node paths, so by actual design this is a “one core” network. However, the founders made this choice and the network was not designed around this reality. We therefore created two special paths for the nodes to provide redundancy. These are as follows: one is a redundancy path and this will be more thoroughly explained in the upcoming posts. The second node is not the route to the network, although a testnet used to run tests.

For each node in the network, we have two redundancy nodes which are also called balancing nodes in the network. These are required to compensate for the nodes that can only provide one service, the router. The three nodes are not replicated because they are only providing the support for the router. In contrast, the additional redundancy nodes cost us nothing in the terms of space or bandwidth. Every node in the ZeroNet network can be one of the following:

Main Path node—points in one of three directions and can be freely chosen.

Mitancy node—points in one of two directions and can be freely chosen.

thanks, Annette!

My most bizarre mold encounter was when I was 7 years old plus. My brother and I were on the beach out by Monterey Bay, huge kelp trees just came up. (We went several times a year there.) The air was foggy, very cold, so I bent down to look at the glassy water but it was pretty briny. Okay, thinking, I may have seen some gnarly moths on the surface, but I didn't think there was anything bad.

Went up vertically and saw a fairly large, very boxy looking moth. I thought the plate-like thing was just some sort of weed. I couldn't believe it and started patty crawling around in the jacuzzi for moulds
